The notebooks below accompany Unit 8. They are ordinary Jupyter notebooks
and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots and `scipy` for a
few of the linear-algebra calls); open them in JupyterLab, VS Code, or any
notebook environment. Dependency-free Python implementations of the two
central algorithms -- the MPC quadratic program solved by projected
gradient descent, and dynamic programming, base-policy evaluation and
rollout for switched systems -- are in [`mpc.py`](mpc.py) and
[`rollout.py`](rollout.py); see [`README.md`](README.md).

## Linear quadratic control with input constraints

The worked example behind §3: a double integrator with the hard constraint
$|u|\leq c$. The notebook sets the problem up as a quadratic program in the
stacked input $\bar u=[u_0\ \cdots\ u_{h-1}]^\intercal$ by eliminating the
state exactly as in Unit 7, then solves it subject to the box constraint.
The thing to try is the comparison that motivates the whole unit: with the
constraint inactive the solution coincides with the Riccati gain of Unit 5
to machine precision, and as $c$ is tightened the input saturates and the
optimal sequence stops being a linear function of the state -- which is why
a policy can no longer be written down in closed form and has to be
recomputed online.

[Download `A_8_LQinputconstraints.ipynb`](A_8_LQinputconstraints.ipynb){download="A_8_LQinputconstraints.ipynb"}

## MPC trajectory tracking for a quadcopter

The application of §3.9. The longitudinal channel of a quadcopter,
$m\ddot p=mg\theta$ and $I_\theta\ddot\theta=\tau$, becomes a fourth-order
integrator after scaling the pitch angle and the torque, and MPC is used to
track a prescribed trajectory in $p$. This is the first notebook in the
course where the horizon is genuinely a design knob you can feel: too short
and the controller cuts corners because it cannot see the turn coming, too
long and it spends effort on a future it will never execute, since only the
first input of each solve is ever applied.

[Download `A_8_A_MPC_quad_tracking.ipynb`](A_8_A_MPC_quad_tracking.ipynb){download="A_8_A_MPC_quad_tracking.ipynb"}

## Control of switched linear systems

The central script for §4, and the one that matches the lecture most
closely. For $x_{k+1}=A_{\sigma_k}x_k$ with the switching signal
$\sigma_k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ as the only decision, exact dynamic programming
represents the cost-to-go as a finite set of quadratic forms whose number
can grow like $m^k$ -- so the notebook builds the exact solution for short
horizons and then the approximate policies (online replanning, MPC,
rollout) that keep the computation bounded, finishing with the
resource-aware control application: deciding at each step which of several
sensors or links to use.

[Download `A_8_SLS.ipynb`](A_8_SLS.ipynb){download="A_8_SLS.ipynb"}

## MPC and rollout for a switched system with disturbances

The stochastic version of the same problem,
$x_{k+1}=A_{\sigma_k}x_k+w_k$ with zero-mean disturbances of covariance
$W$, under the average cost $\lim_h \frac1h\mathbb{E}[\sum_\ell
x_\ell^\intercal Qx_\ell]$. It implements the $H$-step lookahead policy and
compares it with rollout over a base policy. Run it after the previous one:
the disturbances mean the exact cost-to-go is no longer a finite set of
quadratic forms at all, so approximation stops being a matter of
convenience and becomes the only option.

[Download `A_8_K_MPCRollout.ipynb`](A_8_K_MPCRollout.ipynb){download="A_8_K_MPCRollout.ipynb"}
